name: Sam Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at an oil sands mine. It's the size of a house, the bucket holds about a hundred tonnes, and my job is to dig the sand and load the haul trucks, one every two or three minutes. Twelve-hour shifts, and in winter it's thirty below outside while I'm warm in the cab. The trick is loading a truck in four passes without spilling and without the drivers waiting on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been on the shovel?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-two years on the shovel, thirty-four at the mine. I'm the lead operator on my shift, so when there's a new guy, he sits with me. I don't do computers much. My wife Dana handles anything with a password, she's a bookkeeper, and I still have a phone that flips open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much. Maybe that the people who sold it got rich and we got a new screen to ignore. I'd say it in the lunch trailer and that'd be the end of it. I don't go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, good. I've got four years left, maybe three. The house is paid, we've got the cabin up at the lake, and I'd like to get to the end without learning anything new, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I do now. Dig, load, go home. Keep putting money aside and count down to sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's my favourite picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd like to get to the end without learning anything new. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've learned enough. I've had three different control systems on that shovel and each one took me a year to trust. I'm good at what I do, and I'd like to finish being good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you looking forward to at sixty-two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cabin. Fishing, mostly, and fixing the dock that's been leaning for five years. Dana wants to drive down the coast, so we'll do that too.

S0.say: I'd say the people who sold it got rich and we got another screen to ignore. I'd say it in the lunch trailer and that'd be it, because I don't go online.
S0.think: Privately it's good news, with three or four years left, the house paid and the cabin at the lake. I'd like to finish without learning anything new.
S0.do: Carries on digging and loading as now and keeps putting money aside. Counts down to retiring at 62.
S0.feel: Calm, this is his favourite picture.
S0.quote: I've had three different control systems on that shovel and each one took me a year to trust.
S0.fieldNote: Sam speaks in short, dry sentences and wants nothing more than to finish his career unchanged. He is clearly highly skilled and proud of it. His resistance to new technology is open and unembarrassed, partly because he can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go. Every few years something changes at the mine. You get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the haul trucks go first and the shovels come later. They've already got driverless trucks at the next lease over. The shovel's harder, the face is never the same twice. I figure I'd get to sixty-two in the seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much, to start with. I'd watch what happens to the trucks and keep my head down. If they asked me to learn some new system for the shovel, I'd do the minimum to stay in the seat. And if it got silly, I'd go a year early, we can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit tired just thinking about another new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd blame if your job changed under you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The company does what makes money, that's what companies do. The government does what governments do, which is mostly not much. I don't get worked up about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck drivers, the young ones. There's a fellow called Marco who drives for me, nice kid, just bought a house. If the trucks go driverless, he's in trouble.

S1.say: I'd say it's how things go, because every few years something changes at the mine. You just get on with it.
S1.think: Privately I think the haul trucks go first and shovels later, since the face is never the same twice. I figure I'd get to sixty-two still in the seat.
S1.do: Watches what happens to the trucks and keeps his head down, doing the minimum training needed to stay on the shovel. Would retire a year early if it got silly.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little tired at the thought of another new system.
S1.quote: The company does what makes money, that's what companies do.
S1.fieldNote: Sam blames no one and treats change like weather. He is confident his machine will be automated after the trucks, and he may be right. His concern for Marco, a young driver with a new house, was the only sign of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening whether we like it or not, so there's no point shouting. I might say the company moved too fast, if they did. But I'd keep it to the lunch trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be sixty by then and probably finished. I don't like that, because it'd be their choice and not mine. We'd be fine for money, but I'd be sitting at home a couple of years early with nothing to do in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't learn the new stuff. If they said the shovel's going automatic, I'd take the package and go. Before that, I'd stop spending on the new truck I'd been looking at, just to keep things tidy. Then I'd move up to the cabin earlier than planned and fix that dock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. Not about money. More about being shown the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years change things for you, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I don't get to finish. Five or ten, I'm out before the robots arrive at my shovel. With two, I'm the one who leaves early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dana when you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, well, looks like you've got me home sooner. She'd say something about the dock. Then she'd do the numbers on the computer and tell me we're fine, and we would be.

S2.say: I'd say it's happening whether we like it or not, so shouting is pointless. I might say the company moved too fast, but I'd keep it to the lunch trailer.
S2.think: Privately I'd be sixty and probably finished, which I don't like because it would be their choice, not mine. Money's fine, but I'd be home a couple of years early with nothing to do in winter.
S2.do: Takes the package rather than learn a new system if the shovel goes automatic, and holds off on buying a new truck. Moves up to the lake cabin earlier than planned.
S2.feel: A bit anxious about being shown the door, not about money.
S2.quote: With two, I'm the one who leaves early.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline is the only one that touches Sam directly, because it takes away the ending he planned. He would still refuse to learn new systems and simply leave. His worry is about pride and winter boredom, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. Five years is a long time at a mine. Lots of things get announced and never happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, 2031 means I'm already retired, or just about. I'd be sixty-three. I'd probably miss it by a year or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am and retire at sixty-two, like planned. I'd keep an eye on it but wouldn't change anything. If it looked like it was coming quicker, I'd go a few months early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you uneasy, if you'd be retired anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son works at the upgrader, the plant where they process the bitumen. He's thirty-one with two little ones. If everything goes robot in five years, I don't know what he does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to keep some money aside and not buy a bigger house just yet. That's about all I know to say. I'm not the one to tell him about computers.

S3.say: I'd say we'll see, because five years is a long time at a mine and lots of things get announced and never happen. I'd keep it low-key.
S3.think: Privately 2031 means I'm retired or just about, at sixty-three. I'd probably miss it by a year or so.
S3.do: Carries on as he is and retires at 62 as planned, watching the news without changing anything. Would leave a few months early if it came faster.
S3.quote: I'd tell him to keep some money aside and not buy a bigger house just yet.
S3.fieldNote: For himself Sam is mostly untouched, but his unease comes from his son, who works at the upgrader and has two small children. He openly admits he has no advice on technology to give. His scepticism about announcements runs through every answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's somebody else's problem. Sorry, but it is. I'll be fishing at the lake, and the young ones can sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is after I'm gone from the mine. I'd be sixty-eight. It doesn't change anything for me, not one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retire at sixty-two, go to the cabin, drive down the coast with Dana. Nothing to do about it before that. Keep digging until the day I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd want passed on, before the machines take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to read the face. You can see when it's about to slump, the colour changes, little cracks open up. I've taught that to every new operator. I don't know if a machine sees it, and I won't be there to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet at four in the morning, when the pit's all lit up and you're the only one awake for a mile. That's something.

S4.say: I'd say it's somebody else's problem, sorry, but it is. I'll be fishing at the lake by then, and the young ones can sort it out.
S4.think: Privately ten years is after I've left the mine, at sixty-eight. It doesn't change one thing for me.
S4.do: Retires at 62, goes to the lake cabin and drives down the coast with Dana. Keeps digging until his last day with nothing to change before then.
S4.quote: I don't know if a machine sees it, and I won't be there to check.
S4.fieldNote: Sam was completely untroubled by the ten-year picture and said so plainly. His knowledge of reading the dig face is real craft and he has passed it on to every trainee. The image of the lit-up pit at four in the morning showed a quieter side.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. It's the only one that throws me out before I'm ready. What would help? A fair package and a bit of notice. That's all I'd ask for. I can sort out the rest myself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you got it. Maybe ask about the shovel guys specifically. We're the last ones they'll automate, I think, and nobody ever asks us.

headlineQuote: I'm good at what I do, and I'd like to finish being good at it.
portrait: Sam Ziegler is a 58-year-old lead shovel operator at an oil sands mine, with thirty-four years on site, a paid-off house and a cabin at the lake. He avoids new technology, still uses a flip phone, and would rather take a package than learn another control system. He blames no one, seeing companies and governments as doing what they always do. He is calm in almost every picture because he expects to retire at 62 before robots reach his shovel; only AGI by 2028 makes him anxious, because it would push him out early on someone else's terms. His quieter worries are for his son at the upgrader and a young truck driver named Marco.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it is the only picture that would push him out before he is ready.
whatWouldHelp: A fair redundancy package and some notice; he says he can sort out the rest himself.
